```{r}
library(readr) 
library(tidyverse) 
library(ggplot2) 
library(sampling) 
library(survey)
library(robsurvey)
```

```{r}
data(MU284)
```

```{r}
Q1 <- quantile(MU284$P85, 0.25)
Q3  <- quantile(MU284$P85, 0.75) 
IQR <- Q3 - Q1
lower <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR 
upper <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
outliers <- MU284$LABEL[MU284$P85 < lower | MU284$P85 > upper]
MU284$outlier <- ifelse(seq_len(nrow(MU284)) %in% outliers, 1, 0)
```

## Stratum

```{r}
MU284$strate <- cut(MU284$P75, breaks = quantile(MU284$P75, probs = c(0, 1/2, 0.95, 1)), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = c("basse", "moyenne", "haute"))
MU284 <- MU284 %>% mutate(strate_id = case_when(
  strate == "basse" ~ 1,
  strate == "moyenne" ~ 2,
  strate == "haute" ~ 3 ))
```

```{r}
ggplot(MU284, aes(x = P75, y = P85, color = factor(strate))) + 
  geom_point() + 
  labs( title = "Scatter plot entre P75 et P85", x = "Population en 1975 (P75)", y = "Population en 1985 (P85)" ) + 
  theme_minimal()
```

## Sample

#### SRSWOR

```{r}
set.seed(1)
N <- nrow(MU284)
n <- 70

ech_index <- srswor(n, N)
echantillon_srswor <- MU284[ech_index == 1, ]

#create a vector of size n with weight N/n for all element
poids_srswor <- rep(N/n, n)
#create the survey design with weight 
ech.srswor <- svydesign(id=~LABEL, weights=poids_srswor, fpc=rep(N, n), data=echantillon_srswor)
```

#### STSRSWOR

```{r}
N_H <- table(MU284$strate)
# calcul n_h
n <- 70 #choix de n
table(MU284$strate) 
std <- c() 
for (i in 1:3){ 
  std[i] <- sqrt(var(MU284$P85[MU284$strate_id == i])) 
  } 
tab <- table(MU284$strate)*std 
sum_NL <- sum(tab) 
n_H <- n * tab / sum_NL 
round(n_H) #pas ok car n_3 = 34 > N_3 = 15
```

On recommence en fixant $n_3$.

```{r}
n_3 <- table(MU284$strate)['haute'] 
n_12 <- n - n_3
tab <- table(MU284$strate)[1:2] * std[1:2] 
sum_NL <- sum(tab) 
n_H <- n_12 * tab / sum_NL 
n_H['haute'] <- n_3 
n_H <- round(n_H)
n_H
```

### Winsorization

Winsorization with lower and upper bounds : no winsorization for the lower bound and 0.9 percentile for the lower bound

#### Documentation

Characteristic. Population mean or total. Let μ denote the estimated winsorized population mean; then, the estimated winsorized total is given by \$ \\hat{N} \\mu \$ with \$\\hat{N} = \\sum w_i\$ , where summation is over all observations in the sample.

Modes of winsorization. The amount of winsorization can be specified in relative or absolute terms:

-   Relative: By specifying LB and UB, the method winsorizes the LB · 100% of the smallest observations and the (1 - UB) · 100% of the largest observations from the data.

-   Absolute: By specifying argument k in the functions with the "infix" *k* in their name (e.g., svymean_k_winsorized), the largest k observations are winsorized, 0 \< k \< n, where n denotes the sample size. E.g., k = 2 implies that the largest and the second largest observation are winsorized. Variance estimation. Large-sample approximation based on the influence function; see Huber and Ronchetti (2009, Chap. 3.3) and Shao (1994). Two estimators are available:

    -   simple_var = FALSE Variance estimator of the winsorized mean/ total. The estimator de- pends on the estimated probability density function evaluated at the winsorization thresh- olds, which can be – depending on the context – numerically unstable. As a remedy, a simplified variance estimator is available by setting simple_var = TRUE.

    -   simple_var = TRUE Variance is approximated using the variance estimator of the trimmed mean/ total.

```{r}
svymean_winsorized(~P85, ech.stsi, LB = 0, UB = 0.90) #dans la logique il faudrait mettre UB = 0.1 car 1- UB * 100% selon la documentation mais le résultat est très mauvais si on fait ça
```

Winsorization by the k bigger values

```{r}
svymean_k_winsorized(~P85, ech.stsi, k = 5)
```

Try different values of k

```{r}
means_k_winso <- numeric(15)
for (k in 1:15){
  means_k_winso[k] <- coef(svymean_k_winsorized(~P85, ech.stsi, k = k))
}
plot(means_k_winso, ylim = c(23,30), xlab = "Value of k", ylab = "mean")
abline(h = P85_mean, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

```{r}
means_k_winso <- numeric(15)
for (k in 1:15){
  means_k_winso[k] <- SE(svymean_k_winsorized(~P85, ech.stsi, k = k))
}
plot(means_k_winso, xlab = "Value of k", ylab = "SE of the estimated means")
abline(h = P85_mean, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

Optimal R

R solution de \$\\frac{R - \\mu}{n-1} = \\mathbb{E}\_F(max(Y-R,0))\$

On estime l'espérance puis on résoud \$H(R) = \\frac{R - \\mu}{n-1} - {1\\over n} \\sum\_{i=1}\^n max(Y-R,0)) = 0\$

```{r}
mu_pop <- mean(MU284$P85)
n <- length(stsrswor_data)
H_R <- function(R, mu, n, sample){
  terme1 <- (R - mu) / (n - 1)
  terme2 <- sum(pmax(sample - R, 0))/n
  return(terme1 - terme2)
}
R_esp_max <- uniroot(f = H_R, interval = c(min(MU284$P85), max(MU284$P85)),
                     mu = mu_pop, n = n, sample = stsrswor_data$P85)$root
R_esp_max
```

Trouver R

```{r}
MU284 %>% arrange(desc(P85)) %>% select(P85)
```

2 sont supérieurs à R donc k = 2

### Trimmed

#### Documentation

Characteristic. Population mean or total. Let μ denote the estimated trimmed population mean; then, the estimated trimmed total is given by \$\\hat{N} \\mu\$ with \$\\hat{N} = \\sum w_i\$, where summation is over all observations in the sample.

Trimming. The methods trims the LB · 100% of the smallest observations and the (1 - UB) · 100% of the largest observations from the data. Variance estimation. Large-sample approximation based on the influence function; see Huber and Ronchetti (2009, Chap. 3.3) and Shao (1994).

#### Functions

```{r}
svymean_trimmed(~P85, ech.stsi, LB = 0, UB = 0.90)
```

Weighted Huber and Tukey M-estimator of the population mean and total (robust Horvitz-Thompson estimator)

```{r}
mean_huber <- svymean_huber(~P85, ech.stsi, k = 350)
mean_huber
```

```{r}
svymean_tukey(~P85, ech.stsi, k = 350)
```

Essayer les autres paramètres :

-   k [double] robustness tuning constant (0 \< k ≤ ∞).

-   type [character] type of method: "rwm" or "rht".

-   asym [logical] if TRUE, an asymmetric Huber psi-function is used (default: FALSE).

```{r}
svymean_tukey(~P85, ech.stsi, k = 350, type = "rht")
```

```{r}
svymean_tukey(~P85, ech.stsi, k = 3, asym =  TRUE) #asym change rien ?
```

Dalen, see weighted for more details

```{r}
svymean_dalen(~P85, ech.stsi, censoring = 350)
```

```{r}
svymean_dalen(~P85, ech.stsi, censoring = 350, type = 'Z3')
```

Ratio

-   object an object of class [ratio], e.g., result of the Huber ratio M-estimator svyratio_huber.

-   total [numeric] vector of population totals of the auxiliary variables.

-   N [numeric] population size (see also N_unknown.


## Auxiliary information

$T_X$ known

```{r}
sum(MU284$P75)
```

Sampling weights computable : $d_i = 1 / \pi_i$

SRSWOR : $\pi_i = {n \over N}$ then $d_i = {N \over n}$. Dans notre cas : \$d_i = {284 \\over 70}\$

```{r}
sum(echantillon_srswor$P75) * 284/70
#cela doit correspondre à T_X
```

```{r}
set.seed(12)
nsimu <- 1000  
n <- 70
N <- 284
sum_x <- numeric(nsimu)
calibrated_x <- numeric(nsimu)
estimation_y <- numeric(nsimu)
estimation_y_weighted <- numeric(nsimu)

for (i in 1:nsimu) {
  
  ech_index <- srswor(n, N)
  sample_si <- MU284[ech_index == 1, ]
  
  sample_si$weight_si <- rep(N/n, n)
  ech.si <- svydesign(id=~LABEL, weights=~weight_si, fpc=rep(N, n), data=sample_si)
  
  #calibrated estimator on x
  sum_x[i] <- sum(sample_si$P75) * N / n
  calibrated_x[i]<- svytotal(~P75, ech.si)
  
  #estimation of y
  estimation_y[i] <- svytotal(~P85, ech.si)
  estimation_y_weighted[i] <- weighted_total(sample_si$P85, sample_si$weight_si)
  
  
}

print(sum(MU284$P75))
print(mean(sum_x))
print(mean(calibrated_x)) #iso to the previous line
#the estimation is ok then we can use the same weight to compute the T_y
print(sum(MU284$P85))
print(mean(estimation_y))
print(mean(estimation_y_weighted))
#good estimator
```

Then estimators = calibrated total : $\sum_{i \in s} w_i y_i$ and $w_i$ such that $\sum_{i \in s} w_i x_i = T_X$

--\> unbiased but can be inefficient if the model fails (model : $\mathbb{E}_m(y_i | X) = x'_i \beta$ and $\mathrm{Var}_m(y_i|X) \propto \nu_i = x'_i \lambda, i \in U$), especially because of outliers (missclassification bc of outliers)

Regarder les résidus (y - xB) pour voir s'ils ont une forme, ce qui pourrait expliquer la malclassification du modèle

```{r}
#model 
model <- lm(P85 ~ P75, data = sample_si)
beta <- coef(model)['P75']
plot(model$residuals)
```

Decomposition de $\hat{T}_y^C$ permet de montrer que $\hat{T}_y^C - T_y = - \sum_{i \in U - s} (y_i - x'_i - \hat{\beta}^R) + \sum_{i \in s} u_i (y_i - x'_i \hat{\beta}^R) / \sqrt{\nu_i}$

= sampling error : montre que les résidus extrêmes (positif ou négatif) impactent la sampling error

et large $u_i$ + large standardized residual $(y_i - x'_i \hat{\beta}^R) / \sqrt{\nu_i}$ = part importante de la sampling error =\> influential unit =\> obj : réduire le poids de ses unités

Nouvel estimateur : $\hat{T}_y^{RC} = \sum_{i \in s} y_i + \sum_{i \in U-s} x'_i \hat{\beta}^R + \sum_{i \in s} {u_i \over h_i} \psi(h_i \frac{y_i - x'_i\hat{\beta}^R)}{\sqrt{\nu_i}}$

with : $h_i$ weight allowed to depend on both $x_i$ and $d_i$, \$\\psi(t) = t\$ bounded function with \$\\psi (0) = 0\$ and \$\\psi(t= \\approx t\$ when t close to 0. If = for every value of t, \$\\hat{T}\_y\^{RC}\$ reduces the nonrobust calibration estimator

--\> propriété de cet estimateur : census-consistent (no matter the choice of $h_i$ or $\psi(.)$, it reduces to \$T_y\$ if census (s = U or $w_i = 1, \forall i \in U$)

Autre façon d'écrire l'estimateur : skipped (mais lien avec article de Duchesne si bon choix de la huber fonction + ça permet de passer à une type II Winsorization (= two-sided type I Winsorization)

--\> alternatives de l'estimateur ;

-   Lee (1991), in \$\\hat{T}\_y\^C\$, multiply the residual component by \$\\theta \\in [0,1]\$

<!-- -->

-   différents choix de $h_i$ dans la litterature : 1 (Chambers, 1986, 1977), $h_i \propto \sqrt{\nu_i}$ (Gwet and Rivest, 1992), \$h_i = w_i \sqrt{\nu_i}\$ or \$h_i = d_i \\sqrt{\\nu_i}\$ ; \$h_i = u_i = (w_i -1) \\sqrt{\\nu_i}\$

--\> construction of \$\\hat{\\beta}\^R\$ :

-   model-based (relationship between x and y) : should be outlier resistan, high efficiency when model errors are normally distributed then \$\\sum\_{i \\in U - s} x'\_i \\hat{\\beta}\^R\$ little affected by outliers (but substantial bias –\> role of the third term = decrease the bias : $\psi$ brings outliers in the estimation of \$T_y\$)

=\> on espèce compensation entre l'augmentation de la variance et la réduction du biais

-   dans l'autre écriture de l'estimateur (que je n'ai pas réécrit mais (7) dans l'article) : il existe une equation U pour estimer $\beta$ avec \$U(\\beta) = 0\$

    --\> on peut résoudre la dernière équation grâce à GM et on a \$\\hat{T}*y\^{RC} = T'*X \\hat{\\beta}{GM}\$ –\> outlier treatment thanks to the tuning of c de la fonction Huber \$\\psi\$

--\> comparaison entre winsorization et cet estimateur

Winsorization = one-sided Huber function \$\\psi(t) = min(t,R)\$

Stratified sampling design : sous plusieurs conditions (voir p.15, partie 4.2, §2 pour le détail) : $\hat{T}_y^{RC}  = \hat{T}_{yR}$ = winsorized estimator with cutoff $R_h = \hat{\mu}_h + R \frac{f_h}{1 - f_h}$

HT estimator ?

-   if m empty, no auxiliary variable, $\nu_i = 1,\; u_i = h_i = (1/\pi_i - 1)\text{, then }
    \hat{T}_{yR}^{HT} = \sum_{i \in s} \left( y_i + \min\!\big((1/\pi_i - 1)y_i,\, R\big) \right)$

-   if \$m = \mu\$ and $\nu_i = 1$, \$\\sum w_i = N\$ ; if $u_i = h_i = (w_i - 1)$ then robust estimator of µ obtained by estimating \$U(\\beta) = 0\$

    and $\hat{T}_y^{RC} = \sum_{i \in s} w_i \hat{\mu}$

-   HT weights $d_i$, sometimes implicitly calibrated to $T_X$ : true for STSRWOR, probability-propotional-to-size (pps) sampling

--\> choice of the tuning constant : skipped

--\> estimation of the MSE : skipped

--\> implementation of \$\\hat{T}\_y\^{RC}\$

Difficult because of the weights

M1 : weighting approach

$w_i$ replaced by $w_i^R$ robust weights : obtained with the augmented calibration equation : $\sum_{i \in s} w_i^R \begin{pmatrix} x_i \\ y_i \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} T_X \\ \hat{T}_y^{RC} \end{pmatrix}$

M2 : imputation approach

modify $y_i$ (good when a lot of y) : on peut réécrire $\hat{T}_y^{RC} = \sum_{i \in s} w_i y_{. i}$ avec (si fonction de Huber + tuning constant c)

![](images/clipboard-1254235211.png)

avec $s_0$ qui contient les unités qui ont été décrites comme influentes

= type II summetric two-sided regression Winsorized values (estimator : winsorized regression estimator)

![](images/clipboard-3575240895.png)

Easier to interpret : weighted average of the robust predictions $x'_i \hat{\beta}^R$ *and the observed values* $yi$ ; less weight when the observation if highly influential

## Stratum jumpers

Create a observation in not the right strata : big cities in small or medium strata

```{r}
MU284_jump <- MU284 
index <- sample(MU284_jump[MU284_jump$strate == "haute",]$LABEL, 2)
MU284_jump[MU284$LABEL %in% index,]$strate <- "basse" 
MU284_jump[MU284$LABEL %in% index,]$strate_id <- "1" 
MU284_jump$stratum_jumper <- ifelse(MU284_jump$LABEL %in% index, 1, 0)
```

```{r}
ggplot(MU284_jump, aes(x = P75, y = P85, color = factor(strate))) + 
  geom_point() + 
  labs( title = "Scatter plot entre P75 et P85", x = "Population en 1975 (P75)", y = "Population en 1985 (P85)" ) + 
  theme_minimal()
```

### Méthode 1 : winsorized

### Méthode 2 : stratum jumpers
